summary: CERC has proposed that pumped storage plants (PSPs) be allowed to sell in the High Price Day Ahead Market (HP-DAM), which is currently open only to gas stations using imported RLNG or naphtha, imported-coal stations and battery storage. The proposal follows NLDC recommendations of July 2026 and a Ministry of Power letter of 30.07.2026. NLDC's analysis noted that operational PSP capacity (7,425.6 MW) is largely tied up, and that HP-DAM cleared on only 47 days between April 2025 and July 2026. It also found a solar-hour to evening-peak price spread in the DAM of about ₹4.37 per unit. The Commission took the prima facie view that the DAM alone may not give PSPs enough opportunity and that HP-DAM access could improve their viability and support grid flexibility. This is a proposal, not a final order: CERC has started suo motu proceedings, issued a public notice, and asked parties to file written submissions within 15 days of the order dated 28.10.2026.
headline: CERC proposes letting pumped storage plants sell in the high-price day-ahead market

summary: CERC has rejected Vena Energy's plea to treat its 160 MW blended wind project in Koppal, Karnataka (129.6 MW wind, 30.4 MW solar) as a wind generator for deviation settlement. The project was bid under MNRE's 2020 Blended Wind Guidelines and commissioned on 29.10.2024. SRPC treats it as a hybrid because it has wind and solar behind one injection point, which puts it in the tighter deviation band for solar and hybrid sellers under Regulation 8(4) of the DSM Regulations, 2024. Vena said this raised its DSM liability to about 5.3% of revenue, against about 3.0% if treated as wind. The Commission held that qualifying under the Blended Wind Guidelines does not decide treatment under the DSM Regulations. The 33% hybrid threshold in other guidelines is not relevant either, and the developer could have built a wind-only project, as another bidder in the same tranche did. Crucially, the Commission said its powers to relax and remove difficulty under Regulations 11 and 12 cannot be used to create a new category of generating station.

summary: Ambuja Cements Limited built a 150 MW solar plant for captive use across its cement facilities, in the 750 MW solar park of Essel Saurya Urja Company of Rajasthan Limited at Phalodi-Pokhran, Rajasthan. The park's scheduled commissioning date was 30.06.2025. Ambuja said its plant was ready, but allocation of land and the commissioning and charging of the park's pooling station were delayed. summary: NHPC Limited asked the Commission to adopt, under Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003, the tariff for 1,150 MW of additional firm and despatchable renewable power with energy storage. summary: Parighosh Realtors and Developers is developing a 200 MW wind-solar hybrid project in Kutch with connectivity at GETCO's 220 kV Bhachunda substation. GETCO demanded an Associated Transmission System Bank Guarantee (ATS BG) of Rs 20 lakh per MW, Rs 40 crore in total. The developer argued that the 220 kV switchyard and lines were commissioned in December 2020, the substation was state-planned under the Green Energy Corridor, and no new transmission was being built on its account. GETCO said there was no evacuation margin when the application was received, so it was put on hold. It was later processed under Clause 2.2 read with Clause 7.3 of the Connectivity Procedure, 2025, and provisional connectivity was granted on 15.11.2025, subject to system strengthening, with a tentative timeline of December 2027. The Commission held that the earlier commissioning of the 220 kV switchyard does not show that the 200 MW could be evacuated without strengthening. It found that Clause 7.3 covers provisional connectivity under Clauses 5.1(i) and 5.1(ii) and requires the ATS BG. It followed its decisions in Petition Nos. 2626 and 2634 of 2026 and found that GETCO's reliance on Clause 7.3 was not a new ground. The petition was rejected, and the developer must furnish the ATS BG.

summary: Astica Tiles LLP, a tile manufacturer, holds 11 kV connectivity from PGVCL for a 4 MW captive solar plant at Village Liya, Surendranagar. summary: Shri Om Agro Products owns a 1.5 MW wind plant. In 2013 it signed a tripartite wheeling agreement with RVPN and Suzlon Energy covering 0.75 MW for captive use. An amended PPA dated 15.07.2024 moved that 0.75 MW to sale to the discom at Rs 2.44/kWh. RVPN then demanded Rs 15,86,864 in surrender charges under Regulation 14 of the RERC Open Access Regulations, 2016. When the petitioner did not pay, RVPN had the plant disconnected on 28.05.2025. The petitioner argued that these charges compensate only for stranded capacity, and that none existed because the discom now used the same transmission system. The Commission held that Regulation 14(2) sets the charges on a normative basis: 66% of transmission and wheeling charges, for at most three years. Actual stranded capacity therefore need not be shown, and the Commission added that it cannot be assessed with certainty in a meshed network. It read stranded capacity as relinquished capacity and held that the sale to the discom did not waive the liability. It had earlier ordered reconnection on deposit of 25% of the charges, and it now directed the petitioner to pay the balance. summary: Ghatampur Transmission Limited (GTL) sought late payment surcharge (LPS) from Neyveli Uttar Pradesh Power Limited (NUPPL) under Article 10.8.1 of their Transmission Service Agreement, which charges 1.25% per month on a simple rate basis. In an Order dated 14.02.2023, the Commission had held NUPPL liable for GTL's transmission charges and allowed 45 days to pay fresh invoices. NUPPL paid Rs 211.84 crore only on 15.09.2023, after APTEL refused interim relief and the Supreme Court declined to interfere. GTL claimed Rs 22.31 crore up to 30.06.2024. The Commission held the claim was not barred by res judicata or Section 34(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, because the default occurred after the earlier order. Applying the defaulter liability principle did not take the charges outside the agreement, and an appeal without a stay did not suspend the obligation to pay. Even taking the corrected invoice, the due date was 04.05.2023. LPS runs until actual payment, with no LPS charged on accumulated LPS. No LPS applies to the Rs 39.39 crore withheld as liquidated damages from 23.06.2023 to 24.06.2024, when the Commission had permitted that retention. The parties must reconcile the amount invoice by invoice.

outcome: The Commission held that late payment surcharge under Article 10.8.1 is payable on the transmission charges for April to November 2021 until actual payment, and rejected the limitation plea. summary: Obra-C Badaun Transmission Limited sought late payment surcharge (LPS) from UPPCL under Article 10.8.1 of its Transmission Service Agreement (TSA). Monthly transmission charges for Elements 2 to 8 of Lot-1 for April to November 2021 were paid only in February and March 2022. UPPCL argued the invoices were incomplete until UPSLDC certified availability on 11.01.2022. The Commission held that the COD of 16.04.2021, fixed in its 2022 order and upheld by APTEL, is final, and that the duty to pay arises from COD. The Due Date runs from receipt of an invoice, not from its verification. UPSLDC certification is part of finally determining availability, not a condition for payment. UPPCL had not used the TSA's invoice dispute mechanism, and the delay came from the long-term transmission customers insisting on accepting COD first. LPS at 1.25% per month is therefore payable until actual payment. UPPCL's limitation plea for April to July 2021 failed because the dispute arose in February 2022 and the petition was filed on 05.10.2024. Rebate taken on invoices not paid in full, after payments are applied first to LPS, must be reversed. The Letter of Credit prayer had become infructuous.
